messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raj is a 39-year-old interior designer, married for seven years, living in a suburban home that he and his wife Neha had spent months renovating. Three years ago, his younger brother Arun died in a car accident on an interstate highway—a collision that Raj learned about through a phone call from his brother’s phone, a stranger’s voice asking if he could identify the body. He drove to the hospital in a state of frozen disbelief, and in the morgue he saw Arun’s face, intact except for a thin line of dried blood along his hairline, the stillness of his features utterly unlike the brother who had called him the night before to argue about a movie. That image—the cold fluorescent light, the way the sheet was pulled back, the silence—became a fixture in Raj’s mind, replaying without warning.

In the months that followed, Raj tried to resume his life. He threw himself into work, taking on more residential projects than he could reasonably manage. But the flashbacks would come: a sudden sense of being back in that room, the smell of antiseptic, the hollow weight in his chest, his hands going numb as if he were still gripping the hospital railing. He could be standing in a client’s kitchen, discussing tile grout, and in a fraction of a second the world would tilt and he would feel the terror all over again, his body reacting before his mind understood why—his heart hammering, his palms slick, a wave of heat climbing his neck. He learned to excuse himself to the bathroom, splashing cold water on his face, but the irritability that followed was harder to hide. A client’s indecision over cabinet handles could set off a sharp, sarcastic remark that left everyone in the room uncomfortable; Neha’s innocent question about dinner plans could trigger a snapping response that he regretted immediately.

He began to avoid anything that might remind him of Arun. The anniversary of the accident—the third one was approaching—became a date he would mentally block out well in advance, scheduling two full days of back-to-back site visits so he would be too exhausted to think. He stopped attending funerals, even for the fathers of close friends, making excuses about work conflicts until people stopped inviting him. When a colleague mentioned her mother’s recent death, Raj felt his throat close and he changed the subject abruptly, feigning a phone call. He removed all the photos of Arun from his phone and from their apartment; he told Neha it was time to redecorate the living room, replacing the family portraits with abstract prints. He stopped visiting the park where he and Arun used to jog, and he drove an extra fifteen minutes to avoid the street where his brother had lived.

But the avoidance came at a cost. Raj had developed a compulsive ritual of mentally rehearsing the worst-case scenario for any situation. Before every client meeting, he would imagine the project failing, the client suing, his reputation collapsing. Before Neha left for work, he would picture her car rolling on that same interstate, and he would stand at the door listening until he heard the engine fade, only then allowing himself to breathe. He was certain that if he stopped preparing for the worst, the worst would happen—that his vigilance was the only thing keeping disaster at bay. Yet the preparation never made him feel prepared; it only left him wired and exhausted, sleeping poorly and waking with his jaw clenched.

At work, his reputation for fast, creative solutions had eroded. He had declined three commissions in the past year because the clients mentioned designing spaces for a deceased loved one—a memorial garden, a reliquary wall, a bedroom to be kept exactly as it was. The last one had sent him into a panic attack in his car. His boss had started to question his reliability. Neha had begun to withdraw, hurt by his mood swings and by his refusal to talk about Arun at all. She had suggested they attend a Diwali celebration at her sister’s house; Raj had snapped that he didn’t want to see “all those happy families,” and she had left the room in tears.

Three weeks ago, during a home consultation in a client’s sunlit living room, a detail—a particular shade of blue on the wall, the same color as Arun’s favorite T-shirt—triggered a flashback so vivid that Raj sat down on the floor, gasping, convinced for a moment that his brother was about to walk through the door. The client called Neha, and when Raj came home that evening, shattered and ashamed, she told him she could not keep living this way. He agreed to seek help because he was afraid of losing her, but what frightened him most, he admitted to the therapist in his first session, was the idea that the grief would never stop intruding—that he would always be one stray memory away from falling apart. He hoped, without quite believing it possible, that he could someday look at a photograph of Arun and feel only love, not the cold rush of the morgue.
